goal.what: lane's developers know who uses lane and for what, how that user reaches each aim from the first request, and how to tell whether a change made lane better for them, so they design and build lane to give it.
grounds: ux.json purpose: "A UX document describes why users use the product and how they reach that goal. Developers design and build a product that delivers this UX."

decisions.what: Who is lane's user?
decisions.decided: The developer AI: an AI that builds a Claude Code plugin whose subagents work in numbered steps.
grounds: plugins/lane/README.md:6: "lane is for you, an AI that builds a Claude Code plugin whose subagents work in numbered steps."
agreed with the user in the steering's T49

decisions.what: How many objectives, and split by what?
decisions.decided: Two: keeping the rules of each step, and keeping the order the subagents start in. A plugin may want rules with no flow, so each is a job of its own.
grounds: plugins/lane/README.md:3-4 names the two: "keep the rules of their steps and start one another in the order that you set"
plugins/lane/docs/lanes.md and docs/flow.md are written apart; a flow is optional in the proposal

decisions.what: What progress does the developer AI want in O1?
decisions.decided: Its subagents keep the rules written in their numbered steps on every run.
grounds: plugins/lane/README.md:7: "your subagents keep the rules of their steps on every run"

decisions.what: What is the developer AI spared in O1?
decisions.decided: Writing the code that checks the rules.
grounds: plugins/lane/README.md:8: "You write no code for the checks"

decisions.what: O1 as written
decisions.decided: O1: The developer AI wants the subagents of its plugin to keep the rules written in their numbered steps on every run, without writing the code that checks them.
grounds: ux.json Q1 passes example: a user, the progress, the context; no feature of lane named

decisions.what: How is the orchestrator named for a reader who has not met the word?
decisions.decided: The orchestrator, the subagent that starts the others; the order it starts them in is the flow, which the developer AI sets.
grounds: plugins/lane/README.md:8 defines it the same way; the UX is read before the README, so it defines the word where it first appears

decisions.what: What progress does the developer AI want in O2, and what is it spared?
decisions.decided: Its orchestrator starts the others in the order it set, on every run, without a script written for the order.
grounds: plugins/lane/README.md:7-9: "your orchestrator ... starts them in your order ... no script for the order"

decisions.what: O2 as written
decisions.decided: O2: The developer AI wants the orchestrator of its plugin, the subagent that starts the others, to start them in the order that the developer AI set, its flow, on every run, without writing a script for it.
grounds: as D5

decisions.what: What counts each key result, so it cannot rise while the user gets nothing?
decisions.decided: A share of the events that could go wrong, or effort and time the user spends; never a count of output such as checks laid or rules written.
grounds: ux.json Q2 why: "A key result chosen because it is easy to count ... can improve while users get nothing more."
Rodden et al., CHI 2010, Goals-Signals-Metrics

decisions.what: O1: does a break get through?
decisions.decided: KR1.1: the share of tool calls and ends of work that break a rule and still go through; lower is better.
grounds: the signal that the rules are kept on every run, D3

decisions.what: O1: is allowed work stopped?
decisions.decided: KR1.2: the share of tool calls and ends of work that the rules allow but that are stopped; lower is better.
grounds: KR1.1 alone improves by stopping everything; this one holds it to the user's gain

decisions.what: O1: does a stopped subagent go back to its step?
decisions.decided: KR1.3: the share of stopped breaks after which the subagent still does not keep the rule, for example because it tries another way; lower is better.
grounds: plugins/lane/README.md:13-14: "A hook that only refuses a call leaves the subagent to look for another way"; a stop that is routed around keeps no rule

decisions.what: O1: what does the user spend?
decisions.decided: KR1.4: the lines of code the developer AI writes by hand so that its subagents keep the rules; fewer is better. KR1.5: the time from its first rule to the first run in which the subagents keep the rules; shorter is better.
grounds: D4 promises no code written; the time shows what writing a proposal costs

decisions.what: O2: does the orchestrator keep the flow, and is allowed work stopped?
decisions.decided: KR2.1: the share of runs in which the orchestrator leaves the flow; lower is better. KR2.2: the share of the orchestrator's tool calls and ends of work that the flow allows but that are stopped; lower is better.
grounds: a run that leaves the flow at any point fails O2, so KR2.1 counts runs, not calls; KR2.2 holds it as KR1.2 holds KR1.1

decisions.what: O2: what does the user spend?
decisions.decided: KR2.3: the lines of code the developer AI writes by hand so that the orchestrator keeps the flow; fewer is better. KR2.4: the time from its first flow to the first run that keeps it; shorter is better.
grounds: as D13

decisions.what: Which plugin do the scenarios run on?
decisions.decided: The example plugin changelog, which writes a project's CHANGELOG.md, as the README's walkthrough runs it.
grounds: .claude/rules/dev.md step 1: the README takes "the scenario that its walkthrough runs" from the UX
plugins/lane/README.md:62-63

decisions.what: Who takes part in the main paths, and of what kind?
decisions.decided: The developer AI (an AI); lay.py of lane (a script); the check script that lay.py puts into the plugin (a script); the operator who runs the plugin (a person or an AI); changelog's lead, the orchestrator, writer, which writes new entries into CHANGELOG.md, and reviewer, which compares the entries with the commits (AIs).
grounds: ux.json Q3: whether each is a person, an AI or a script tells which steps wait for a person
only those that act on a main path; lay.py up and Python missing are off it

decisions.what: What does the developer AI do first in O1?
decisions.decided: It asks lay.py print for two rules on step 3 of writer: write only CHANGELOG.md, do not run git commit or git push; and sees step 3 with the sentence of each rule.
grounds: plugins/lane/README.md:62-89; scripts/steps.py:61 prints the step as it will be

decisions.what: How does it end its part?
decisions.decided: Once it approves what print showed, it runs lay.py write, which writes the sentences into step 3 and puts the check script into changelog.
grounds: plugins/lane/README.md:91-101

decisions.what: Where does O1 reach its aim?
decisions.decided: The operator runs changelog; writer writes CHANGELOG.md and the check script lets it through; writer runs git commit, the check script stops it with "changelog: Do not run `git commit` or `git push`.", and writer ends with CHANGELOG.md written and no commit.
grounds: hooks/lane/hook.py:163 heads each sentence with the plugin's name; guard.py:233-234 tells the step's sentence, and hands_off adds no line (lanes/hands_off.py:15)

decisions.what: What does the developer AI do first in O2?
decisions.decided: It asks lay.py print for the flow writer, reviewer, back to writer when reviewer answers `more`, and sees the flow and its sentence on step 1 of lead; then lay.py write writes the sentence and puts the check script into changelog.
grounds: plugins/lane/docs/flow.md:9-12: the sentence "Take each move lane tells you, until it tells none."

decisions.what: What is lead told as it starts, and after each subagent?
decisions.decided: As it starts: "changelog: The next move of the flow is move 1: start `changelog:writer`." After reviewer answers `more`: "changelog: reviewer answered `more`. The next move of the flow is move 1: start `changelog:writer`." Once reviewer answers otherwise: "changelog: The flow is done: lane tells no more moves."
grounds: hooks/lane/moves.py:105-115 gives each line; called.py:185,199 tells it; hook.py:163 heads it with the plugin's name

decisions.what: Which stop belongs on the main path, and where does O2 reach its aim?
decisions.decided: lead tries to end after writer, and the check script stops it with "changelog: Take each move lane tells you, until it tells none." and, on the next line, "The next move of the flow is move 2: start `changelog:reviewer`."; writer and reviewer go again until reviewer does not answer `more`, and lead ends with the reviewed entries.
grounds: an early end is the slip an orchestrator makes most and shows the flow held; guard.py:233-234 puts the move on the line after the sentence; lanes/follow_flow.py:34

decisions.what: What does the document leave to the architecture?
decisions.decided: Only what the developer AI and the operator do, see and get; no hook event, file of the plugin or module of lane.
grounds: ux.json Q4 why: "Internal design written here is decided twice, drifts from the architecture document"

decisions.what: How is each message shown?
decisions.decided: As its exact text, so a developer reads what the user sees and a change to the text shows as a change to the UX.
grounds: what the user reads is the UX; a paraphrase cannot be checked against the code

decisions.what: How does the check script appear?
decisions.decided: As one participant that lets calls through, stops them and tells lead its moves, named as the README names it, the check script.
grounds: plugins/lane/README.md:115: "lane puts its checks into your plugin as one script, the check script"; the hooks it runs by are the architecture's

decisions.what: Which words does the document use for what lane holds?
decisions.decided: rule, step, flow, move and orchestrator, each said in everyday words where it first appears; lane's own word lane is not used.
grounds: the README says rule for what docs call a lane (plugins/lane/README.md:12); the user of the UX has not met lane's terms
